lessons.title: The EASIEST Way To Get Better At UI Design In Figma
objectives: Practise in a way that actually improves your eye
Build a habit you can keep alongside other work
lessons.notes:
Improvement in visual design comes from one thing: looking closely at good work and rebuilding it, repeatedly. Not from tutorials, which teach the tool rather than the eye.

THE METHOD, and it works: choose a screen from an app that is genuinely well made, and REBUILD IT FROM SCRATCH without downloading anything. You will be forced to notice the spacing between the price and the title, the exact weight of the heading, why the button is that height. Those noticings are the skill. Passive watching produces none of them.

DO IT SMALL AND OFTEN. One screen, forty minutes, three times a week beats a weekend of one enormous project, because improvement comes from the number of times you make the judgement, not the hours spent.

THEN CHANGE SOMETHING. After rebuilding faithfully, redesign it for a different purpose - the same screen for an older user, or with half the content, or for a business selling something else. That is where copying becomes designing.

WHAT TO LOOK AT: apps people actually use every day rather than design-site showpieces. Showpieces are built to be looked at and often could not survive real content, real names of varying length, or an empty state.

KEEP EVERYTHING YOU MAKE. A folder of forty rebuilt screens is both visible progress and the raw material for a portfolio.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - rebuild the apps YOUR users use, because that is where your advantage is. Study the Kenyan products people open every day - the mobile money flows, the banking apps, the local marketplaces, the transport and delivery apps - and notice which parts work and which parts everybody complains about. You will learn more about designing for this market from one careful rebuild of a payment confirmation screen than from ten foreign showpieces. It also gives you something to say in front of a client that no imported portfolio can match. And practise with REAL CONTENT: long Kenyan names that do not fit a neat field, prices in shillings with thousands separators, descriptive addresses rather than a house number and postcode. Designs break on real content, and that is exactly what you want to discover in practice rather than in production.
lessons.practice: Rebuild one screen from a Kenyan app you use daily, from scratch, without downloading anything, and note every spacing and weight decision you had to make. Then redesign the same screen for half the content and for a user with the system font enlarged. Do this three times this week and keep all of it.

quiz.question: What actually improves your eye?
options: Rebuilding good screens from scratch, repeatedly, and noticing the decisions

quiz.question: Why study apps people use daily rather than design showpieces?
options: Showpieces often could not survive real content, varying name lengths or an empty state

lessons.title: 7 UI/UX Design Mistakes that I Wish I Knew as a Beginner
objectives: Recognise the mistakes that mark work as inexperienced
Fix each one with a specific change
Catch them yourself before a client does
lessons.notes:
The mistakes are consistent across beginners, which means they are all fixable and all worth checking before you show anything.

TOO MANY COLOURS AND TYPEFACES. One main colour, a neutral range, three status colours. One typeface in three or four sizes. Restraint reads as confidence, and variety reads as indecision.

INCONSISTENT SPACING. Gaps of 13, 17 and 22 because things were dragged. Pick a unit and use multiples of it. This single change does more than any other to make work look professional.

NO HIERARCHY. When everything is the same size and weight, the eye has nowhere to go. Every screen should have one obviously most important thing.

CROWDING. Beginners fill the space. White space is what makes the important thing visible.

DESIGNING WITH PERFECT CONTENT. Neat names, three-word titles, flattering photographs. Real content is long, missing, and badly shot, and a layout that only works with perfect content does not work.

IGNORING STATES. The screen exists as loading, empty, failed and successful. Designing only the successful one leaves the other three to be invented by whoever builds it.

LOW CONTRAST. Pale grey on white looks refined on a good screen in a dark room, and is unreadable everywhere else.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the two mistakes that specifically cost money in this market, both of which sit underneath the seven above. DESIGNING FOR A DEVICE NOBODY HAS: a design built on a large recent phone with fast connection and tested on nothing else will fail on the mid-range Android with a smaller screen and an enlarged system font that most of your users hold. Check it there before you show it. And FORGETTING THE COST OF WEIGHT: a designer who specifies a full-screen video, three typefaces and uncompressed photographs has spent the user's money and lost the slower half of the audience, and no amount of visual quality compensates. Both are the same error - designing for the conditions you are working in rather than the conditions the design will live in.
lessons.practice: Take one design you have already made and check it against all seven, fixing each with a specific change. Then open it on a mid-range Android with the system font enlarged, outdoors, and list everything that fails there. Fix those too.

quiz.question: Which single change does most to make work look professional?
options: Consistent spacing from one repeating unit

quiz.question: What underlies both of the mistakes that cost money in this market?
options: Designing for the conditions you work in rather than the conditions the design will live in

lessons.title: E-Learning App UI/UX Design in Figma (Wireframe & Prototype)
objectives: Take one app from flow to prototype end to end
Design the screens that carry the real work of the product
Produce something that belongs in a portfolio
lessons.notes:
This is the applied project. Follow the build, then do it again for a product you understand, because the second one is where you are designing rather than following.

THE ORDER, which matters: the flow first - what a learner does from arriving to finishing a lesson - then wireframes of each step, then the visual design, then the prototype. Jumping to visual design is what produces a set of handsome screens that do not connect.

THE SCREENS THAT CARRY A LEARNING PRODUCT: browse, so someone can tell what is on offer and what it costs; the course page, which has to answer what you get, how long, and what happens after; the lesson itself, which is where the user spends nearly all their time and which beginners design last and least; progress, which is what brings people back; and payment, which is where the money is won or lost.

DESIGN THE LESSON SCREEN PROPERLY. It is the product. Where does the video sit, how is the written material read, how does the person mark it done and get to the next one without hunting.

INCLUDE THE UNGLAMOROUS SCREENS: empty states before anything is started, the moment a purchase fails, and what someone sees when they return after three weeks away.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - design this one for the learner who is actually going to use it here. THE VIDEO IS THE EXPENSIVE PART on a bundle, so the design should say how long something is and let the learner choose when to spend the data, rather than autoplaying and surprising them. Written notes alongside the video are not a secondary feature here, they are the part a learner returns to when they cannot afford to stream again - so give them real space rather than a collapsed panel. PAYMENT IS M-PESA: design the handoff and the return, including what the learner sees if the prompt never arrives, because that is the commonest way a real enrolment is lost. And design PROGRESS TO SURVIVE INTERRUPTION - people study in short pieces between other work, so continuing exactly where you stopped is worth more than any badge.
lessons.practice: Design the app end to end in order - flow, wireframes, visual, prototype - for a product you understand. Give the lesson screen the most attention, include the empty, failed and returning-after-weeks states, and design the payment handoff and return. Then test the prototype on a phone with three people.

quiz.question: Which screen do beginners design last and least, wrongly?
options: The lesson screen, where the user spends nearly all their time

quiz.question: Why give written notes real space in a learning app here?
options: They are what a learner returns to when they cannot afford to stream again
They replace the need for video

lessons.title: Create a Full Website Design in Figma
objectives: Design a complete site rather than a single page
Make each page do one job in the visitor's journey
Hand a design over so it can be built
lessons.notes:
A website is a set of pages with different jobs, and the commonest failure is designing a beautiful home page and treating everything else as an afterthought.

WHAT EACH PAGE IS FOR:
HOME answers who this is for, what they get, and what to do next, above the fold and in plain words. Most home pages fail this.
THE SERVICE OR PRODUCT PAGE is where the decision is made and is usually the most visited page from search. Give it the attention the home page normally gets.
ABOUT is read by people deciding whether to trust you, so real photographs and real names beat stock imagery.
CONTACT should be the easiest page on the site and is frequently the worst.

DESIGN THE NARROW LAYOUT FIRST, as Module 5 covered, and use the styles and components you built rather than making fresh decisions on every page.

CONSISTENCY ACROSS PAGES is what separates a site from a folder of designs: the same header, the same spacing, the same button, the same type scale everywhere.

HANDING IT OVER TO BE BUILT: name the frames, include every state, specify the fonts and the exact colours, export the images at the right sizes, and write down anything that is not visible in the file - what happens when a form is submitted, what the error says, what is behind a menu. A developer who has to guess will guess differently from what you intended.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - design for how this site will actually be reached and used. MOST VISITS WILL BE ON A PHONE FROM A SOCIAL LINK OR A SEARCH, arriving on an interior page rather than the home page, so every page must independently say who this is and what they do. The most important element on a small business site here is a TAPPABLE PHONE NUMBER OR WHATSAPP BUTTON, visible without scrolling, because the conversion is a conversation and not a form. Specify COMPRESSED IMAGES and be willing to tell a client that the full-width video header they want will cost them visitors on a bundle. And design the CONTACT AND DELIVERY INFORMATION for how things work here - an area and a landmark rather than a postcode, a phone number that someone answers, and delivery terms stated plainly, because that is what a cautious buyer is looking for before they commit.
lessons.practice: Design a four-page site - home, service, about, contact - narrow width first, using one set of styles and components. Put a tappable phone or WhatsApp action above the fold on every page. Then write the handover note: fonts, colours, image sizes, every state, and what happens after the form is submitted.

quiz.question: Which page usually deserves the attention the home page gets?
options: The service or product page, where the decision is made and search traffic lands

quiz.question: What is the most important element on a small business site here?
options: A tappable phone or WhatsApp action visible without scrolling

lessons.title: How to Get Freelance Clients as a UX/UI Designer
objectives: Find design work that is realistically winnable here
Sell an outcome rather than a set of screens
Set terms that protect the work and get you paid
lessons.notes:
Design freelancing splits into a contested international market and an underserved local one, and most people here will start locally whatever they intend.

THE LOCAL REALITY: few businesses are looking for a UI/UX designer. They are looking for more enquiries, a shop people can order from, or something that does not embarrass them when they send a link. Sell that. The screens are how you deliver it.

WHERE THE WORK IS, in order of realism:
BUSINESSES WITH A BAD OR NO SITE, which you can see for yourself.
DEVELOPERS AND AGENCIES who build but do not design, and who bring repeat work rather than one job.
STARTUPS AND SMALL SOFTWARE TEAMS, who need product design and usually have budget.
NGOS AND PROGRAMMES needing tools, forms and reporting screens.
BUSINESSES ALREADY ADVERTISING, since they are spending on marketing and are losing it at a bad page.
ONLINE PLATFORMS, crowded and low-priced, useful for early reviews.

WHAT WINS THE JOB: not a portfolio of imagined apps, but showing you understand their problem. Redesign one screen of their actual site or product before the conversation, and lead with what is wrong and what it costs them.

SCOPE IT BEFORE YOU START. Number of screens, number of revision rounds, what a new screen costs. Design attracts opinions, and unlimited revisions turn a fair price into a bad one.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - three local realities. Many clients ASK FOR A WEBSITE WHEN THEY NEED SOMETHING ELSE - a properly set up WhatsApp catalogue, a working local business profile, and two good pages will earn them more than a handsome site nobody visits. Say so; the honesty wins the relationship and the next job. Second, GET A DEPOSIT before you design and the balance before final files are handed over, on M-Pesa, with the scope written in the WhatsApp thread, and hand over source files only when paid - this is the commonest place designers here lose money. Third, PARTNER WITH DEVELOPERS EARLY: they are asked for design constantly, they do not want to do it, and one good relationship produces more steady work than any amount of advertising.
lessons.practice: Pick three local businesses whose site or product is clearly failing them. Redesign one screen of each before making contact, and lead with what is wrong and what it costs them. Write your scope terms - screens included, revision rounds, price of an extra screen - and your deposit terms, before you speak to anyone.

quiz.question: What wins a local design job?
options: Showing you understand their problem, often by redesigning one screen of their real product first
A large portfolio of imagined apps
A lower price than other designers

quiz.question: When should source files be handed over?
options: Before the deposit, to build trust

lessons.title: UX/UI Portfolio + Case Study Full Course
objectives: Build a portfolio that shows thinking rather than pictures
Write a case study with a real problem and a real outcome
Present work honestly when the project was small or unbuilt
lessons.notes:
A portfolio of attractive screens gets you compliments. A portfolio of case studies gets you hired, because a client is buying judgement and needs to see it.

THREE OR FOUR PROJECTS IS ENOUGH. Depth beats quantity every time, and a weak fifth project drags down the impression of the other four.

THE CASE STUDY STRUCTURE THAT WORKS:
THE PROBLEM, in the client's or user's words. Specific, not "they needed a modern redesign".
WHAT YOU FOUND OUT, however small - five people asked, a look at the existing numbers, a walkthrough of the old thing.
THE DECISIONS YOU MADE AND WHY. This is the whole case study. Not what you designed, but what you chose between and on what grounds. Include something you tried and rejected.
WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE, which is where the screens finally appear.
WHAT HAPPENED. Enquiries, completion rate, time to finish a task, or what the client said. If nothing was measured, say so plainly.

WRITE FOR SOMEONE SKIMMING. Headings that carry the story, short paragraphs, and the outcome near the top.

IF THE PROJECT WAS NEVER BUILT, say so. Nobody minds. What they mind is discovering it later.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - making this work for the clients you will actually meet. MOST LOCAL CLIENTS WILL NOT READ A LONG CASE STUDY, so carry two versions: the full write-up for agencies and international applications, and a one-screen before-and-after with a single sentence of outcome for the small business owner on WhatsApp. The second wins more local work than the first. Second, MAKE IT OPENABLE ON A PHONE, on a bundle - a heavy portfolio site with large images is a portfolio nobody sees, and a lightweight page or even a well-made PDF beats an impressive slow one. Third, USE REAL LOCAL WORK EVEN WHEN IT IS SMALL: a redesign of a real shop's ordering flow, with the owner's comment about what changed, is more persuasive here than an imagined banking app, and it proves you have dealt with real content, real constraints and a real person's opinions.
lessons.practice: Write one full case study using the five-part structure, including a decision you rejected and an honest statement about what was or was not measured. Then produce the short version - one before-and-after screen and a single sentence of outcome - and send it to someone on WhatsApp to check it reads on a phone.

quiz.question: What is the heart of a case study?
options: The decisions you made and why, including something you tried and rejected

quiz.question: What wins more local work than a long case study?
options: A one-screen before-and-after with a single sentence of outcome
